chunks: Musa ibn al-Qasim narrated from Muhammad ibn Sa'id from Isma'il ibn Abi Ziyad from Abu Abdillah from his father, peace be upon them both, who said:

Ali (peace be upon him) said: If a person in ihram and a person not in ihram kill game together, he said: 'Upon the one in ihram is the full ransom, and upon the one not in ihram is half the ransom. And this is only obligatory upon the one not in ihram if his game is in the Haram (sanctuary). As for if his game is in the Hill (non-sanctuary), there is nothing upon him.'

And whoever slaughters game, upon him is a sheep. And if a group ate it, upon each one of them is a sheep. One person narrated: 'The blood of a sheep, and you all share in it, because that was from you unintentionally. And if that was from you intentionally, causing the game to fall and then falling, I would obligating upon each one of you the blood of a sheep.'
Abu Wallad said: That was from us before we entered the Haram.

key_terms.حَرَمٌ: Sanctuary (specifically the sacred area of Mecca)
key_terms.فِدَاءٌ: Ransom or compensation for a religious violation
key_terms.مُحِلٌّ: One not in the state of ihram
key_terms.مُحْرِمٌ: One in the state of ihram (sacred consecration for Hajj/Umrah)

ai.seo_question: What is the fidyah ruling for a person not in ihram who kills game with someone in ihram?
ai.summary: Imam Ali (AS) establishes a nuanced distinction in fidyah based on the location of the kill relative to the Haram and the state of ihram, noting that non-muhrims are exempt if the game is in the Hal. The hadith further elucidates the principle of proportional liability for groups, differentiating between unintentional sharing (where one sheep suffices for all) and intentional consumption (where each member bears individual liability), reflecting the juristic focus on intent (niyyah) in Shia fiqh. This ruling is foundational for understanding the economic and ritual penalties in Hajj jurisprudence.
